newsitem.title: CROATIA: Zagreb frees Serb POWs under new amnesty law.
newsitem.headline: Zagreb frees Serb POWs under new amnesty law.

text.p: Croatia, acting on a new general amnesty law, has released around a hundred minority Serbs detained for rebelling against the state, Croatian and Serbian media reported on Monday.
The Belgrade daily Politika said about a hundred members of Serb paramilitary units were released from the county jail in Split over the weekend.
But 18 other Serbs charged with war crimes remained in custody of the Split district court, the daily said.
The amnesty law, which took effect last Saturday, pardons all minority Serbs who took part in an uprising against Croatia's declaration of independence in 1991, except those charged with war crimes.
Most of those released were taken in buses to Serbia, and a few opted to stay in Croatia, the Croatian state news agency HINA said.

In their rebellion backed by the former Yugoslav federal army, Croatian Serbs expelled Croats from one third of the country and carved out a self-styled state they called Krajina, which survived four years.
Zagreb recaptured most of the Krajina in two blitz offensives across truce lines in 1995, prompting up to 200,000 Serbs to flee to Serb-held Bosnia and Serbia.
The United Nations administers the remaining sector, known as Eastern Slavonia, and is due to transfer it back to Zagreb's control next year.
